711.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor.”
711.explanation: Guru Nanak makes the worth of speech depend on its effect: only words that bring honour are approved.
711.tie_back: The Kural asks the clean-minded speaker to weigh his words before speaking; Guru Nanak likewise says speech must be weighed by whether it brings honour.
711.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
711._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both ask for weighed speech, but Gurbani's honour is honour before God, and it says nothing about first sizing up the assembly.

712.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
712.explanation: In a trader's maxim, Guru Nanak says one must first understand what one is dealing with before committing to the transaction.
712.tie_back: The Kural says the speaker should understand the matter fully before speaking; Guru Nanak gives the same order: understand first, then act.
712.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
712._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the maxim matches 'understand fully, then act', but it is about choosing one's spiritual dealings, not about speech or the right moment.

713.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
713.explanation: Guru Nanak dismisses excessive talk as empty babble.
713.tie_back: The Kural says one who speaks without understanding the assembly shows no real ability; Guru Nanak calls speech that is not grounded in understanding mere useless babble.
713.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanasri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
713._accuracy_note: Next-best: a general warning against idle talk, not specifically against speaking without knowing one's audience.

714.quote_or_event: “If you are wise, be simple; if you are powerful, be weak; … How rare is one who is known as such a devotee.”
714.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, praises the rare devotee who hides wisdom and strength under simplicity.
714.tie_back: The Kural tells the learned to take on the plain colour of white plaster among the dull and keep their brilliance hidden; Farid likewise says the wise should appear simple.
714.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 128) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
714._accuracy_note: A strong fit on concealing one's wisdom, though Farid commends it as a devotee's lasting humility while the Kural recommends it as tactics before a dull audience.

715.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
715.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very essence of all good qualities.
715.tie_back: The Kural calls the restraint that does not rush to speak first before wiser elders the best of all good things; Guru Nanak names humility the essence of virtue.
715.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
715._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both rank humility first among virtues, but Gurbani does not speak specifically of deferring in speech to elders.

716.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation.”
716.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that careless, graceless speech spoils the speaker inwardly and ruins his name.
716.tie_back: The Kural compares a slip of speech before the deeply learned to losing one's footing on the path; Guru Nanak says bad speech brings a fall in one's whole standing.
716.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
716._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the salok is about harsh or insipid speech in general, not a single slip before a learned audience.

717.quote_or_event: “They alone purchase the gem, O Nanak, who have virtue in their purse. Those who do not appreciate the value of the jewels, wander like blind men in the world.”
717.explanation: Guru Angad says the jewel (the Name and the Guru's word) is valued only by those qualified to recognise it; others pass it by like the blind.
717.tie_back: The Kural says learning shines only among those able to judge words flawlessly; Guru Angad says jewels are prized only by those who can appraise them.
717.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
717._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on worth recognised only by qualified judges; the jewel in Gurbani is the Name, not scholarly learning.

718.quote_or_event: “The Word is the tree; the garden of the heart is the farm; tend it, and irrigate it with the Lord's Love.”
718.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the Guru's word as a tree planted in the garden of a receptive heart and watered with love.
718.tie_back: The Kural likens speaking to people who understand to watering a bed where plants are already growing; Guru Nanak likewise pictures the word flourishing in a watered, prepared heart.
718.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 354, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
718._accuracy_note: Next-best: the garden-and-watering image is shared, but in Gurbani the watering is love for God within the hearer, not a speaker addressing a receptive audience.

719.explanation: Guru Nanak's brief counsel in Asa ki Vaar is not to waste words in dispute with the foolish.
719.tie_back: The Kural tells those who speak well in good assemblies never, even by forgetfulness, to speak in a mean one; Guru Nanak likewise says not to spend words on fools.
719.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (pauri 19), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
719._accuracy_note: A strong practical parallel, though Gurbani speaks of arguing with fools rather than of choosing which assembly to address.

720.quote_or_event: “If you take Ambrosial Nectar and irrigate the neem tree with it, still, says Kabeer, its natural qualities are not changed.”
720.explanation: Bhagat Kabir pictures nectar poured on the bitter neem: the nectar is wasted and the neem stays bitter. Commentators such as Sahib Singh read the hymn as warning against pressing spiritual teaching on the unreceptive.
720.tie_back: The Kural likens speaking before those not of one's kind to nectar spilled into a gutter; Kabir likewise shows nectar wasted on something that cannot receive it.
720.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
720._accuracy_note: A strong fit, with the same image of wasted nectar; Kabir stresses the unchanging nature of the recipient rather than the unclean place, and the 'unreceptive hearer' reading comes from commentary.
